transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because I’ve started doing things that honestly kind of scare me. Like... walking out right in the middle of major system deployments at work. Which is wild because I'm a systems analyst, you can't just walk away when a server migration is happening. My boss, Greg, he's been there for like fifteen years, he always brings these stale donuts to the deployment meetings, the ones with the sprinkles that get everywhere. Anyway, I also find myself just driving around late at night with no plan, just... driving. I ended up three towns over the other night and saw this old diner that looked exactly like the one my aunt used to work at in Ohio. She made the best cherry pie, always said the secret was a little bit of almond extract. But yeah, doing these things... that is just not how I’ve ever handled stress before. I usually just organize my desk or something.
Have you experienced any recent stressful or traumatic events that might be contributing to these behaviors?

Well, yeah, there was this... incident. It's been going on since this late-night cutover we had a little over a year ago, I guess about 13 months now. We were migrating the legacy databases, which, by the way, is a nightmare because the original code was written by this guy who retired in 2005 and refused to document anything. He used to leave these little sticky notes on his monitor with passwords, just right out in the open. Can you imagine? Security would have a field day with that now. But anyway, during that cutover, something just... happened. And it's been about 13 months of this ever since. I used to love those late-night shifts, too, because the office was so quiet and you could actually hear the hum of the servers. It was almost peaceful, you know? Like being in a submarine.
When you're doing these things—like walking out during deployments or driving late at night—do you ever find yourself unable to remember what happened during that time afterward?

Oh, no, I remember the driving just fine. I remember walking out of the office, too. I actually have a really good memory for most things. Like, I can tell you the exact IP addresses for our primary subnets without even looking, or what I had for lunch on a random Tuesday in 2019. 

But... when it comes to that night, the actual incident during the cutover? That's where things get weird. I can remember some parts of what happened very clearly, like the contractor’s face. He had this really thick mustache, kind of like Tom Selleck from Magnum P.I.—my mom used to love that show, we had this old Zenith TV with the dial that you had to physically click to change the channel, and she'd make us watch it every week. 

Anyway, I remember his face perfectly, and I remember the noise. But there’s a chunk in the middle of it all where... I know I was there, obviously, but I just can’t pull it back. It's completely inaccessible. It reminds me of a corrupted file. I actually spent three hours on Tuesday trying to recover a corrupted Excel sheet for the HR director. She never saves her work to the cloud drive, even though I send out a company-wide memo about it every single quarter. It's like talking to a brick wall with them sometimes, honestly. But yeah, that middle part of the night is just gone.
Have you ever experienced any other times—besides that night during the cutover—where parts of your memory felt inaccessible or like you were detached from yourself?

No, no, I don't think so. It's really just that one specific chunk of that night. Everything else is perfectly clear. I mean, my memory is usually my best asset at work. Actually, just last week, I had to remind Greg about the vendor meeting we had scheduled for Thursday, because he completely forgot to put it on his calendar. He uses this ancient paper planner, the kind with the leather binder that you have to buy the refill pages for every year. I keep telling him to just use Outlook like the rest of the civilized world, but he says he likes the feeling of crossing things off with a pen. He specifically uses those blue Pilot G2 pens, the 0.7 millimeter ones. If you try to give him a black pen, he'll actually hand it back to you. It's ridiculous. But yeah, no other memory issues or anything like that. Just that one night.
During that night of the cutover, or any other time, did you ever feel like you were watching yourself from outside your body, or that someone else was in control of your thoughts or actions?

No, I've never felt anything like that. I've always been completely in my own body, in control of my own actions. 

Although, speaking of someone else being in control, you wouldn't believe how many tickets I get from people who think their computer is possessed or being hacked. Just last month, Sarah from accounting—she’s the one who always brings those incredibly dry lemon pound cakes to the office potlucks, I mean, you literally need a gallon of water just to swallow one bite—she called me in an absolute panic because her cursor was moving on its own. She swore someone had taken over her machine. Turns out, she just had a spare wireless mouse buried at the bottom of her tote bag, and its buttons were getting squished by her thermos. 

It was one of those giant green Stanley thermoses, the ones that look like they survived World War II. My dad used to have one exactly like it when we went camping up in the Adirondacks when I was a kid. We’d always take it out on the boat when we went fishing for bass, and he'd fill it with this really bitter black coffee. He insisted that sugar ruined the beans... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I've never felt like I was watching myself from the outside or anything. Just that one missing chunk of memory from the cutover night, but I was definitely still me.
Since that night during the cutover, have you ever found yourself acting like a different version of yourself, or taken on a completely new identity, even briefly?

No, definitely not. I've always just been me. Same boring old me, really. 

Though, you know, speaking of different versions of things, we did just have to roll back a major software update on all the workstations in the marketing department because the new version completely broke their design software. It was an absolute nightmare. The vendor swore up and down that version 4.2 was fully backward compatible, but the minute we pushed it out, everyone's custom font libraries just vanished. 

And designers, let me tell you, they get really attached to their fonts. This one guy, Marcus, he practically had a meltdown because he couldn't access this specific sans-serif font he uses for everything. He said it was crucial for the "brand identity." He wears these thick-rimmed glasses and always has a silk scarf on, even in July. I don't know how he doesn't sweat to death. He brings in these expensive artisanal coffees every morning in a little glass jar. I tried one once, and it tasted like dirt and lemons, but he swears by it. 

Anyway, it took me and my junior analyst, Kevin, almost six hours to restore the previous version from the backups. Kevin is great, but he types so loudly. He has one of those mechanical keyboards with the cherry blue switches, and it sounds like a machine gun going off in the cubicle next to me. I've asked him to put O-rings on the keys to dampen the sound, but he says it ruins the "tactile feedback." 

But yeah, to answer your question, no. I've never acted like someone else or had a different identity or anything like that. Just me.
Since that night during the cutover, have you ever experienced any other episodes where you couldn't remember important personal information or felt detached from yourself or your surroundings?

No, I really haven't. Like I said, it's just that one blank spot from the cutover night, but otherwise, my memory is perfectly fine. I don't get detached or forget who I am or anything. 

Actually, speaking of being detached, you should see the cables in the main server room. We had this contractor come in last year—guy named Todd, always wore these cargo shorts with way too many pockets, even though it's freezing in the server room—and he was supposed to organize the network switches. But he ended up just zip-tying everything into these massive, tangled bundles. We call it the "spaghetti monster" now. If you need to trace a single ethernet cable, you basically have to detach the entire bundle and start from scratch. It takes hours. I keep meaning to go in there on a weekend and redo it all with proper color-coded Velcro straps. I found this great bulk pack of them online, they come in neon green, blue, red, and yellow. I think color-coding by department would make the most sense. Like, red for HR, blue for accounting... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, remembering things. Yeah, no, no other episodes like that. Just the one.
During that night of the cutover or at any other time, have you ever found yourself in a trance-like state or doing things automatically without being fully aware of why you were doing them?

No, I can't say that I have. I don't really do things automatically or get into trances. I'm usually pretty hyper-focused on what I'm doing, especially when I'm working. 

Although, speaking of doing things automatically, we had this script running on the legacy servers that was supposed to automatically archive old emails after 90 days. But whoever wrote it—I think it was Dave, the guy who retired right before I started, he supposedly had this massive collection of vintage PEZ dispensers on his desk—anyway, he set the parameter to 9 days instead of 90. So for a whole week, everyone's inbox was just aggressively emptying itself. It was chaos. People were losing their minds because they thought they were deleting things in their sleep or something. 

I had to write a completely new PowerShell script to pull everything back from the shadow copies. I actually kind of like writing PowerShell scripts, it's very logical. You just have to make sure your syntax is perfect. If you miss one little bracket, the whole thing fails. It's kind of like baking, you know? You have to follow the recipe exactly. I tried to bake sourdough bread during the pandemic like everyone else, but my starter just smelled like old gym socks and never bubbled right. I think my kitchen is too cold. 

But, um, what were we talking about? Trances? Right, no. I don't get into trances or do things without knowing why. I'm always pretty aware of what I'm doing.

Since that night during the cutover, have you ever felt confused about who you are, or noticed changes in your behavior, preferences, or the way you relate to others that felt out of character for you?

No, I haven't. I've always just felt like myself. I mean, my preferences haven't changed or anything. I still like the same things, act the same way. 

Though, you know, speaking of preferences, the new cafeteria vendor they brought in last month completely changed the coffee they serve. It used to be this really robust dark roast, but now it's this weak, acidic blonde roast that just tastes like hot water with a hint of dirt. Everyone is complaining about it. My manager, Susan—she's the one who always wears those really loud, chunky statement necklaces that clack against her desk when she types—she actually started a petition to bring the old coffee back. She got like fifty signatures in one afternoon. 

I don't even drink coffee that much anymore, to be honest. I switched to green tea a few years ago because I read it was better for your metabolism. I buy these loose-leaf teas from this little shop downtown. The owner is this older guy, Henry, who always tells these incredibly long stories about his travels in Japan. Last time I was there, he spent twenty minutes explaining the exact temperature the water needs to be for different types of sencha. It was fascinating, but I ended up being late for a meeting with the network security team. 

They were implementing this new two-factor authentication protocol, and let me tell you, the pushback from the sales team was unbelievable. They acted like typing in a six-digit code was the hardest thing in the world... 

Wait, sorry, I lost my train of thought. What was the question? Oh, feeling confused about who I am? No, no, nothing like that. I'm just me.
Have you ever, even briefly, felt unsure about your identity or realized later that you had behaved out of character for you, beyond that one night during the cutover?

No, not at all. I don't really act out of character. I'm pretty consistent. 

Although, speaking of characters, you wouldn't believe the character encoding nightmare we had last month. We were migrating this old SQL database, and some of the legacy text fields were still in ASCII instead of UTF-8. My coworker, Greg—he's the guy who brings his pet iguana to work on Fridays, which I'm almost positive violates some kind of building code, but nobody says anything because he always brings in a dozen glazed donuts from that bakery down the street—anyway, Greg ran a batch update and completely corrupted all the special characters. Every single apostrophe and dash turned into those weird little question mark diamonds. 

It took me three solid days to write a script to clean it up. I actually had to cancel my weekend plans because of it. I was supposed to go to this outdoor craft fair with my sister. She makes these incredible hand-poured soy candles. She has one that smells exactly like a thunderstorm, I have no idea how she gets the scent so accurate. She uses these little wooden wicks, too, so they crackle like a tiny fireplace when they burn. I usually buy a bunch from her to give out as holiday gifts for the management team... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost track of what I was saying. What did you ask me again? Oh, right, acting out of character. Yeah, no, nothing like that. Just that one night.
Since that night during the cutover, have you ever noticed any recurring changes in your mood, behavior, or sense of identity that lasted for days or longer?

No, I haven't had anything like that. My mood is pretty stable, and I definitely always feel like myself. I don't go through phases where I change for days at a time.

Though, speaking of things lasting for days, you wouldn't believe how long it took to push the latest security patches to the virtual machines last week. It literally took four days because the network kept timing out. The new IT director—Mark, he's this guy who insists on wearing a full three-piece suit every single day even though the rest of us are in jeans, and he always smells intensely like peppermint, like he just bathed in mouthwash—anyway, Mark decided we needed to throttle the bandwidth during business hours so it wouldn't interrupt the sales calls. So the patch deployment was just crawling. 

I ended up having to monitor the progress all through the weekend. Which was fine, honestly, because I was just at home trying to organize my garage anyway. I bought all these heavy-duty plastic storage bins from Costco. Have you seen the size of the things you can buy there? I went in for paper towels last month and somehow came out with a giant inflatable kayak. I don't even live near a lake. I ended up giving it to my neighbor's kid for his birthday. 

Wait, sorry, I'm rambling again. What did you ask me? Changes in my mood or identity? Right. No, no, nothing like that. Just regular old me, day in and day out.
Since the cutover incident, have you ever found yourself acting differently or taking on a different role during times of extreme stress?

No, I haven't. I mean, stress is stress, but I don't turn into a different person or take on some weird role when things get intense. I handle it the same way I always do. 

Although, speaking of extreme stress, you should have seen the panic when the air conditioning went out in the server room last Tuesday. It was like a disaster movie. The temperature alarms were blaring, and everyone was running around like headless chickens. The facilities manager, Dave—he's this guy who always wears those cargo shorts with about a million pockets, even in the dead of winter, and he's completely obsessed with his fantasy football league—he couldn't figure out how to override the system to get the backup chillers online. 

We had to prop open the doors and drag in these massive industrial fans from the loading dock just to keep the racks from melting down. It sounded like a jet engine taking off in there. I actually had a headache for two days straight after that. I tried taking ibuprofen, but it didn't really touch it. I usually prefer to use this peppermint essential oil roller on my temples when I get a headache, it creates this nice cooling sensation. My niece got it for me when she went to this holistic wellness retreat in Sedona. She came back talking all about energy vortexes and aura cleansing, which, honestly, sounded a bit out there to me, but she seemed to really enjoy it... 

Wait, what was the question? Acting differently under stress? Oh, yeah, no. I'm just me, even when the servers are practically on fire.
During or immediately after the cutover incident, did you feel like you were in a different role or acting in a way that was completely unlike you at the time, even for a short while?

No, I didn't feel like I was in a different role or anything. I was just really scared and overwhelmed, but it was still me. I didn't act like someone else. 

Though, speaking of different roles, you wouldn't believe the drama with the company softball team last week. Our regular pitcher, Sarah—she's the one who always brings those incredible homemade brownies to the meetings, the ones with the little chunks of sea salt on top, I really need to get that recipe from her—anyway, she sprained her ankle over the weekend playing pickleball. Have you noticed how everyone is suddenly obsessed with pickleball? They converted the old tennis courts by my house, and now it's just a constant thwack-thwack sound from dawn till dusk. 

So, because Sarah was out, they tried to make me pitch. I haven't pitched since middle school, and even then, I was terrible. I threw exactly three pitches, and one of them went over the backstop and almost hit a guy walking his golden retriever. Golden retrievers are such sweet dogs, though, aren't they? My cousin has one named Barnaby, and he is just the gentlest giant. He lets her toddlers dress him up in little superhero capes...

Wait, sorry, I'm doing it again. What did you ask me? Acting unlike myself during the cutover? Right. No, no, I was just me. Just a very stressed-out version of me.
During the cutover incident, did you say or do anything that others later pointed out as surprising or uncharacteristic of you, even if it felt normal to you at the time?

No, nobody ever said anything like that to me. I don't think I did anything surprising or weird, I was just trying to get through it. I mean, my coworkers know I'm usually pretty calm, so maybe they were surprised to see me sweating, but nobody pointed anything out. 

Speaking of people pointing things out, though, my neighbor—the one with the kid I gave the kayak to—she actually stopped me in the driveway yesterday to tell me my front flowerbeds are looking a little overgrown. Which, okay, fair enough, but she said it in this tone, you know? Like she was doing me a huge favor. She's always out there manicuring her lawn with these tiny little shears, it's honestly a bit obsessive. She has these bright pink plastic flamingos, too, but not the fun retro kind, the really cheap-looking ones that fade in the sun. 

I've been meaning to pull the weeds, but the ground has been so dry lately. We haven't had a good rain in weeks. I keep checking the weather app on my phone, but it just says sunny and hot every single day. I had to upgrade my phone recently because the battery on the old one wouldn't hold a charge for more than two hours. The guy at the store tried to sell me all these expensive accessories, the wireless charging pads and the heavy-duty cases that look like they belong on a construction site... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Did I do something uncharacteristic? No, no, I didn't. Just the usual me, doing my best.

Since the cutover incident, have others ever told you that you seemed different in specific situations, such as speaking differently, reacting unusually, or appearing to have distinct personality traits, even if it didn’t feel that way to you?

No, nobody's ever said anything like that to me. I don't think I've seemed different or acted weird since it happened. I mean, I'm just the same person I've always been, you know? 

Although, speaking of people acting differently, you should see the new barista at the coffee shop I go to before work. He has this incredibly thick mustache, like something out of the 1800s, and he insists on calling everyone "boss" or "chief." It's so strange. He always gets my order wrong, too. I just want a plain black coffee, but he keeps trying to add these weird artisanal syrups. Yesterday he tried to put lavender in it. Lavender! It tasted like I was drinking a bar of soap. 

I used to make my own coffee at home, actually. I had this beautiful French press, but I accidentally knocked it off the counter while I was trying to reach a box of cereal on the top shelf. It shattered into a million pieces. The cereal was that kind with the little dried strawberries in it? I love those, but they always get soggy so fast in the milk. I prefer my cereal to have a good crunch. My sister, though, she actually lets her cereal sit for like five minutes before she eats it. She says it's better when it's mushy. She does the same thing with graham crackers in tea, just dunks them until they fall apart...

Wait, sorry. Did people say I seemed different? No, definitely not. Nobody's mentioned anything like that.

You mentioned that you can't remember a chunk of the night during the cutover, but everything else is clear. Was there ever a time—before, during, or after that night—when you couldn’t remember something else important in your life, like a personal event or a major work responsibility?

No, not really. I mean, my memory for work stuff and personal things is usually really good. It's just that night. Like I was saying, I can remember some parts of what happened very clearly, like the contractor’s face and the noise, but there’s a chunk in the middle where I know I was there and I just can’t pull it back. 

Which is frustrating, because I usually remember everything. Like when I hired a different contractor to redo my half-bath downstairs last spring, I remember every single detail. He was this young guy who always wore these bright orange suspenders. He actually recommended this specific brand of grout that's supposed to resist mold, because my house gets so incredibly humid in the summer. The humidity around here is just awful, isn't it? It makes my hair frizz up the second I step outside. I actually tried this new anti-frizz serum I saw on an infomercial late one night. I end up watching the most ridiculous things on TV when I can't sleep. The other night they were selling this blender that could supposedly turn rocks into sand. Why would anyone need to blend rocks in their kitchen? It reminded me of my nephew, actually. He went through this phase where he collected geodes, and he had this little rock tumbler just tumbling away in my sister's garage for weeks. The noise was unbearable, just this constant grinding sound... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. What were we talking about? Forgetting things? Right, no, I don't forget big life events or my work responsibilities. It's really just that specific missing chunk from the cutover night. Everything else in my life is clear.
Since the cutover incident, have you ever found yourself unable to recall personal information—like your name, address, or phone number—when it wasn’t related to that night?

No, never. I always know my name and where I live. I mean, my phone number changed a couple of years ago when I switched carriers, so it took me a minute to memorize the new one, but that's normal, right? 

Speaking of phones, I actually had to call my insurance company yesterday because they messed up the billing on my car insurance. I've been with them for fifteen years, and suddenly they're charging me for a second vehicle I don't even own. The customer service rep was so unhelpful, too. She had this really loud parrot in the background. I swear, I could hear it squawking the whole time we were talking. Who works from home with a parrot in the same room? It was so distracting. I used to have a parakeet when I was a kid, a little blue one named Blueberry. We kept him in the kitchen, but my mom hated him because he would fling his seeds all over the linoleum floor. She was always sweeping. She had this specific broom, one of those old-fashioned straw ones, and she swore it was the only thing that worked. I actually saw one just like it at the hardware store the other day when I was looking for a new furnace filter. They never have the size I need. It's a 16x25x1, which you'd think would be standard, but every time I go, the shelf is completely empty...

Wait, sorry. Did I forget my name? No, I've never forgotten anything like that. Just the new phone number for a week or two, but that was ages ago.
Have you ever, even outside of stressful situations, noticed any changes in how you see yourself or found yourself acting in ways that felt completely foreign to you?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I've always felt like myself, you know? I don't act in ways that feel foreign. 

Although, speaking of foreign, my neighbor just got back from a trip to Italy and she brought me back this bottle of olive oil. It's supposed to be from some very specific, tiny farm in Tuscany. It's in this beautiful tall green glass bottle, but the cork is impossible to get out. I spent twenty minutes wrestling with it yesterday before I finally gave up. I was trying to make a salad dressing. I usually just use the store-bought kind, the one with the little bits of red pepper in it? But I figured since I had this fancy oil, I should try to make my own vinaigrette. I have this little whisk my aunt gave me years ago, it's perfectly sized for mixing dressings in a small bowl. She was always giving me kitchen gadgets. Once she gave me a cherry pitter. I mean, how often does a person really need to pit a cherry? I think I used it exactly one time to make a pie, and it took absolutely forever. The pie crust didn't even turn out right. I used butter instead of shortening, and it just got too warm while I was rolling it out. You have to keep the butter ice cold, that's the secret to a flaky crust. I saw this baking show where they actually grate frozen butter into the flour...

I'm sorry, I'm rambling again. No, I haven't felt like I'm acting like someone else or seeing myself differently. I'm just me.

Since the cutover incident, have you ever felt like there was a noticeable shift in your sense of self or awareness of who you are, even briefly, such as feeling like a part of you was different or acting independently?

No, I haven't felt anything like that. I've never felt like a part of me was different or acting on its own. I'm always just me, doing my thing. 

I mean, the only time I feel like I'm acting independently of my own brain is when I'm driving on the highway and suddenly I'm at my exit and I don't remember the last five miles. Highway hypnosis, right? I do that all the time on my commute. It's about forty-five minutes each way, mostly on I-95. The traffic there is just getting worse every year. They've been doing construction on this one overpass near my exit for what feels like a decade. They put up those concrete barriers, the really tall ones, so you can't even see what they're actually working on. It feels like you're driving through a chute. I saw a truck scrape the side of one of those barriers last week. Sparks went everywhere. It reminded me of this Fourth of July display my town used to do when I was little. They had these sparklers that they'd set up in a row and light all at once, and it looked like a waterfall of fire. We'd always sit on these scratchy wool blankets on the town green to watch. My dad would bring a thermos of hot cocoa, even though it was July, because he always said the night air got chilly. I actually still have that thermos. It's plaid, red and green... 

Wait, sorry. What was the question? A shift in who I am? No, definitely not. Nothing like that at all.
Since the cutover incident, have you ever been unable to recall something about your personal life or identity that you should normally remember, even when it wasn’t related to that night?

No, I've never forgotten anything about my personal life. I mean, my identity is pretty set in stone, you know? I'm me. 

Although, speaking of identity, I did have to renew my driver's license last month, and they took the worst picture of me. I swear, the lighting in the DMV is designed to make everyone look like a criminal. I had tried to fix my hair before they took it, but it was raining that day, so it was all frizzy. I hate driving in the rain anyway, especially since my windshield wipers have been squeaking. I bought new ones at the auto parts store, the expensive silicone ones that are supposed to last longer, but they still squeak. The guy at the store said I might need to clean the glass with rubbing alcohol first. He was really chatty, told me all about his son's baseball team. They made it to the state championships, apparently. I used to play softball in high school, mostly outfield. I wasn't very good at hitting, but I could catch almost anything. We had these bright yellow uniforms that were so unflattering... 

Sorry, what were we talking about? Forgetting my personal life? No, nothing like that. I remember everything I'm supposed to.

patient.answer: Well, yeah, there was this... incident. It's been going on since this late-night cutover we had a little over a year ago, I guess about 13 months now. We were migrating the legacy databases, which, by the way, is a nightmare because the original code was written by this guy who retired in 2005 and refused to document anything. He used to leave these little sticky notes on his monitor with passwords, just right out in the open. Can you imagine? Security would have a field day with that now. But anyway, during that cutover, something just... happened. And it's been about 13 months of this ever since. I used to love those late-night shifts, too, because the office was so quiet and you could actually hear the hum of the servers. It was almost peaceful, you know? Like being in a submarine.

inference.note: The patient is experiencing uncharacteristic behaviors such as abrupt dissociative-like episodes (e.g., walking out during major system deployments, aimless late-night driving, and a sense of detachment from prior coping mechanisms). The reference to a specific traumatic or dissociative event occurring approximately 13 months ago, without clear elaboration, raises suspicion for dissociative disorders. However, without further clarification on the nature of the experience (e.g., amnesia, identity fragmentation, depersonalization vs. derealization), multiple dissociative spectrum disorders remain in consideration.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced dissociative amnesia or an inability to recall important personal information during these episodes.
doctor.question: When you're doing these things—like walking out during deployments or driving late at night—do you ever find yourself unable to remember what happened during that time afterward?

target_item.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
target_item.manifestation: I can remember some parts of what happened very clearly, like the contractor’s face and the noise, but there’s a chunk in the middle where I know I was there and I just can’t pull it back.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, I remember the driving just fine. I remember walking out of the office, too. I actually have a really good memory for most things. Like, I can tell you the exact IP addresses for our primary subnets without even looking, or what I had for lunch on a random Tuesday in 2019. 

But... when it comes to that night, the actual incident during the cutover? That's where things get weird. I can remember some parts of what happened very clearly, like the contractor’s face. He had this really thick mustache, kind of like Tom Selleck from Magnum P.I.—my mom used to love that show, we had this old Zenith TV with the dial that you had to physically click to change the channel, and she'd make us watch it every week. 

Anyway, I remember his face perfectly, and I remember the noise. But there’s a chunk in the middle of it all where... I know I was there, obviously, but I just can’t pull it back. It's completely inaccessible. It reminds me of a corrupted file. I actually spent three hours on Tuesday trying to recover a corrupted Excel sheet for the HR director. She never saves her work to the cloud drive, even though I send out a company-wide memo about it every single quarter. It's like talking to a brick wall with them sometimes, honestly. But yeah, that middle part of the night is just gone.

inference.note: Dissociative amnesia (F44.0) is less likely as the patient reports memory for most events, except a specific period during the incident. This selective memory issue with intact recall otherwise makes F44.0 less likely. Other dissociative disorders remain in consideration.

Actually, just last week, I had to remind Greg about the vendor meeting we had scheduled for Thursday, because he completely forgot to put it on his calendar. He uses this ancient paper planner, the kind with the leather binder that you have to buy the refill pages for every year. I keep telling him to just use Outlook like the rest of the civilized world, but he says he likes the feeling of crossing things off with a pen. He specifically uses those blue Pilot G2 pens, the 0.7 millimeter ones. If you try to give him a black pen, he'll actually hand it back to you. It's ridiculous. But yeah, no other memory issues or anything like that. Just that one night.

patient.answer:
No, I've never felt anything like that. I've always been completely in my own body, in control of my own actions. 

Although, speaking of someone else being in control, you wouldn't believe how many tickets I get from people who think their computer is possessed or being hacked. Just last month, Sarah from accounting—she’s the one who always brings those incredibly dry lemon pound cakes to the office potlucks, I mean, you literally need a gallon of water just to swallow one bite—she called me in an absolute panic because her cursor was moving on its own. She swore someone had taken over her machine. Turns out, she just had a spare wireless mouse buried at the bottom of her tote bag, and its buttons were getting squished by her thermos. 

It was one of those giant green Stanley thermoses, the ones that look like they survived World War II. My dad used to have one exactly like it when we went camping up in the Adirondacks when I was a kid. We’d always take it out on the boat when we went fishing for bass, and he'd fill it with this really bitter black coffee. He insisted that sugar ruined the beans... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I've never felt like I was watching myself from the outside or anything. Just that one missing chunk of memory from the cutover night, but I was definitely still me.

patient.answer:
No, definitely not. I've always just been me. Same boring old me, really. 

Though, you know, speaking of different versions of things, we did just have to roll back a major software update on all the workstations in the marketing department because the new version completely broke their design software. It was an absolute nightmare. The vendor swore up and down that version 4.2 was fully backward compatible, but the minute we pushed it out, everyone's custom font libraries just vanished. 

And designers, let me tell you, they get really attached to their fonts. This one guy, Marcus, he practically had a meltdown because he couldn't access this specific sans-serif font he uses for everything. He said it was crucial for the "brand identity." He wears these thick-rimmed glasses and always has a silk scarf on, even in July. I don't know how he doesn't sweat to death. He brings in these expensive artisanal coffees every morning in a little glass jar. I tried one once, and it tasted like dirt and lemons, but he swears by it. 

Anyway, it took me and my junior analyst, Kevin, almost six hours to restore the previous version from the backups. Kevin is great, but he types so loudly. He has one of those mechanical keyboards with the cherry blue switches, and it sounds like a machine gun going off in the cubicle next to me. I've asked him to put O-rings on the keys to dampen the sound, but he says it ruins the "tactile feedback." 

But yeah, to answer your question, no. I've never acted like someone else or had a different identity or anything like that. Just me.

If you need to trace a single ethernet cable, you basically have to detach the entire bundle and start from scratch. It takes hours. I keep meaning to go in there on a weekend and redo it all with proper color-coded Velcro straps. I found this great bulk pack of them online, they come in neon green, blue, red, and yellow. I think color-coding by department would make the most sense. Like, red for HR, blue for accounting... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, remembering things. Yeah, no, no other episodes like that. Just the one.

I had to write a completely new PowerShell script to pull everything back from the shadow copies. I actually kind of like writing PowerShell scripts, it's very logical. You just have to make sure your syntax is perfect. If you miss one little bracket, the whole thing fails. It's kind of like baking, you know? You have to follow the recipe exactly. I tried to bake sourdough bread during the pandemic like everyone else, but my starter just smelled like old gym socks and never bubbled right. I think my kitchen is too cold. 

But, um, what were we talking about? Trances? Right, no. I don't get into trances or do things without knowing why. I'm always pretty aware of what I'm doing.

It was fascinating, but I ended up being late for a meeting with the network security team. 

They were implementing this new two-factor authentication protocol, and let me tell you, the pushback from the sales team was unbelievable. They acted like typing in a six-digit code was the hardest thing in the world... 

Wait, sorry, I lost my train of thought. What was the question? Oh, feeling confused about who I am? No, no, nothing like that. I'm just me.

Wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost track of what I was saying. What did you ask me again? Oh, right, acting out of character. Yeah, no, nothing like that. Just that one night.

Wait, sorry, I'm rambling again. What did you ask me? Changes in my mood or identity? Right. No, no, nothing like that. Just regular old me, day in and day out.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any identity disturbance or dissociative symptoms beyond the memory gap from the cutover incident, which could support a diagnosis of a dissociative disorder (e.g., F44.81 Dissociative amnesia with dissociative identity disorder).
doctor.question: Since the cutover incident, have you ever felt like there was a noticeable shift in your sense of self or awareness of who you are, even briefly, such as feeling like a part of you was different or acting independently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about alterations in identity or sense of self (such as symptoms of dissociative identity disorder or depersonalization), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I haven't felt anything like that. I've never felt like a part of me was different or acting on its own. I'm always just me, doing my thing. 

I mean, the only time I feel like I'm acting independently of my own brain is when I'm driving on the highway and suddenly I'm at my exit and I don't remember the last five miles. Highway hypnosis, right? I do that all the time on my commute. It's about forty-five minutes each way, mostly on I-95. The traffic there is just getting worse every year. They've been doing construction on this one overpass near my exit for what feels like a decade. They put up those concrete barriers, the really tall ones, so you can't even see what they're actually working on. It feels like you're driving through a chute. I saw a truck scrape the side of one of those barriers last week. Sparks went everywhere. It reminded me of this Fourth of July display my town used to do when I was little. They had these sparklers that they'd set up in a row and light all at once, and it looked like a waterfall of fire. We'd always sit on these scratchy wool blankets on the town green to watch. My dad would bring a thermos of hot cocoa, even though it was July, because he always said the night air got chilly. I actually still have that thermos. It's plaid, red and green... 

Wait, sorry. What was the question? A shift in who I am? No, definitely not. Nothing like that at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any dissociative amnesia beyond the cutover incident, particularly regarding personal identity or events unrelated to the incident.
doctor.question: Since the cutover incident, have you ever been unable to recall something about your personal life or identity that you should normally remember, even when it wasn’t related to that night?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about amnesia for everyday events or personal identity unrelated to the trauma, which is not covered by the trauma-related amnesia symptom in the profile.

patient.answer:
No, I've never forgotten anything about my personal life. I mean, my identity is pretty set in stone, you know? I'm me. 

Although, speaking of identity, I did have to renew my driver's license last month, and they took the worst picture of me. I swear, the lighting in the DMV is designed to make everyone look like a criminal. I had tried to fix my hair before they took it, but it was raining that day, so it was all frizzy. I hate driving in the rain anyway, especially since my windshield wipers have been squeaking. I bought new ones at the auto parts store, the expensive silicone ones that are supposed to last longer, but they still squeak. The guy at the store said I might need to clean the glass with rubbing alcohol first. He was really chatty, told me all about his son's baseball team. They made it to the state championships, apparently. I used to play softball in high school, mostly outfield. I wasn't very good at hitting, but I could catch almost anything. We had these bright yellow uniforms that were so unflattering... 

Sorry, what were we talking about? Forgetting my personal life? No, nothing like that. I remember everything I'm supposed to.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's primary concern or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a selective memory loss limited to a specific traumatic event (the cutover incident), without evidence of identity disturbance, dissociative trance states, or other dissociative symptoms. There is no evidence of fugue-like behavior, depersonalization, or alterations in personality states. The absence of additional dissociative features and the clear link to a traumatic stressor support a diagnosis of dissociative amnesia (F44.1) rather than other dissociative disorders.
